citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the policy-induced path laws below. Let $S$ be a nonempty finite state set, let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty action set for each $s\in S$, and let $\mathcal R\subset\mathbb R$ be a finite nonempty reward set. A finite Markov decision process here consists of these sets and a joint next-state/reward probability mass $p(s',r\mid s,a)\ge0$, defined for $s,s'\in S$, $a\in A(s)$, and $r\in\mathcal R$, with $\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}p(s',r\mid s,a)=1$ for every $(s,a)$. A stationary Markov policy $\sigma$ assigns probabilities $\sigma(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sigma(a\mid s)=1$ at every state.

Fix a horizon $H\ge1$, a discount $0\le\gamma\le1$, and an initial state $s_0\in S$. A trajectory is a tuple $\tau=(s_0,a_0,r_1,s_1,\ldots,a_{H-1},r_H,s_H)$ with $s_t\in S$, $a_t\in A(s_t)$, and $r_{t+1}\in\mathcal R$ for each $0\le t<H$. Write $\Omega_H$ for the finite set of all such tuples. For each stationary policy $\sigma$, let $P^\sigma_H$ be the probability law on $\Omega_H$ whose atom masses are

$$P^\sigma_H(\{\tau\})=\prod_{t=0}^{H-1}\sigma(a_t\mid s_t)p(s_{t+1},r_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t).$$

For a trajectory $\tau$, its finite-horizon return is $G_H(\tau)=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^t r_{t+1}$, and the value of target policy $\pi$ from $s_0$ is $J_H(\pi;s_0)=\int_{\Omega_H}G_H\,dP^\pi_H$. A fixed logged dataset of size $n\ge1$ consists of independent trajectories $(\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_n)$, each with law $P^\mu_H$ for a behavior policy $\mu$; the true behavior propensities $\mu(a\mid s)$ used to generate the data are known. Full horizon coverage means $P^\pi_H\ll P^\mu_H$, so every behavior-null trajectory event is also target-null. In this finite setting, the condition $\pi(a\mid s)>0\Rightarrow\mu(a\mid s)>0$ at every state-action pair reachable under $\pi$ before time $H$ is sufficient for full horizon coverage. A trajectory function is integrable under a law $P$ when $\int_{\Omega_H}|f|\,dP<\infty$. All returns are integrable in this finite-horizon finite-reward setting; importance-weighted return expressions below are used only when they are integrable.

Assume AC for the policy-induced trajectory laws. Input a finite-horizon logged dataset of $n\ge1$ independent behavior trajectories, a target policy $\pi$, the true behavior propensities $\mu(a\mid s)$, horizon $H$, and discount $0\le\gamma\le1$. Require full horizon coverage $P^\pi_H\ll P^\mu_H$. For trajectory $i$, compute $\rho_{i,t}=\pi(A_t^i\mid S_t^i)/\mu(A_t^i\mid S_t^i)$ for $0\le t<H$, and $W_{i,t}=\prod_{k=0}^{t}\rho_{i,k}$; set $W_{i,-1}=1$. If an observed pair has $\mu(A_t^i\mid S_t^i)=0<\pi(A_t^i\mid S_t^i)$, return status unsupported; if both probabilities are zero, set that ratio to zero. Let $G_i=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^tR_{t+1}^i$. Return the ordinary trajectory estimator

$$\widehat J_{\mathrm{OIS}}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n W_{i,H-1}G_i,$$

the per-decision estimator

$$\widehat J_{\mathrm{PDIS}}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^tW_{i,t}R_{t+1}^i,$$

and the self-normalized weighted estimator

$$\widehat J_{\mathrm{WIS}}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{i=1}^nW_{i,H-1}G_i}{\sum_{i=1}^nW_{i,H-1}},&\sum_{i=1}^nW_{i,H-1}>0,\\0,&\sum_{i=1}^nW_{i,H-1}=0.\end{cases}$$

All three outputs are finite under the finite-MDP, finite-horizon and coverage hypotheses. The procedure specifies estimators; it includes no finite-sample unbiasedness assertion for the self-normalized output.

Assume AC and the finite-horizon dataset conditions of the preceding definition, with full horizon coverage $P^\pi_H\ll P^\mu_H$. For $0\le t<H$, let $\Omega_{t+1}$ be the finite set of trajectory prefixes through $(R_{t+1},S_{t+1})$, and let $P^\sigma_{t+1}$ be the marginal law of this prefix under policy $\sigma\in\{\pi,\mu\}$. On a behavior-positive prefix define

$$W_{0:t}=\prod_{k=0}^{t}\frac{\pi(A_k\mid S_k)}{\mu(A_k\mid S_k)},$$

and set $W_{0:t}=0$ on behavior-null prefixes. Then $P^\pi_{t+1}\ll P^\mu_{t+1}$, and $W_{0:t}$ is a version of $dP^\pi_{t+1}/dP^\mu_{t+1}$ up to $P^\mu_{t+1}$-almost-everywhere equality. In particular, for every real $G$ integrable under $P^\pi_H$, the full-horizon weight $W_{0:H-1}$ satisfies

$$\mathbb E_{P^\mu_H}[W_{0:H-1}G]=\mathbb E_{P^\pi_H}[G],\qquad \mathbb E_{P^\mu_H}[W_{0:H-1}|G|]<\infty.$$

The same identity holds prefixwise: for each $0\le t<H$ and every real $g$ integrable under $P^\pi_{t+1}$, with $g$ evaluated on the observed prefix,

$$\mathbb E_{P^\mu_H}[W_{0:t}g]=\mathbb E_{P^\pi_H}[g],\qquad \mathbb E_{P^\mu_H}[W_{0:t}|g|]<\infty.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: Fix a logged trajectory index $i$. By [F1], its law is $P^\mu_H$, and [F3] applied to $G_i$ gives $\mathbb E_\mu[W_{i,H-1}G_i]=\mathbb E_\pi[G_H]=J_H(\pi;s_0)$. Linearity [F4] gives $\mathbb E_\mu[\widehat J_{\mathrm{OIS}}]=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nJ_H(\pi;s_0)=J_H(\pi;s_0)$.

Fix $i$ and $0\le t<H$. The reward $R_{t+1}^i$ is a function of the prefix through $(R_{t+1},S_{t+1})$, so [F3] gives $\mathbb E_\mu[W_{i,t}R_{t+1}^i]=\mathbb E_\pi[R_{t+1}]$. Multiplying each equality by the fixed $\gamma^t$ and summing the finite range $0\le t<H$, [F4] yields $\mathbb E_\mu[\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^tW_{i,t}R_{t+1}^i]=J_H(\pi;s_0)$.

Each of the $n$ PDIS trajectory scores in [F2] has expectation $J_H(\pi;s_0)$ by step 1.2. Their finite sample average has the same expectation by [F4], proving $\mathbb E_\mu[\widehat J_{\mathrm{PDIS}}]=J_H(\pi;s_0)$. Step 1.1 proves the ordinary-estimator claim.

Each return and every finite sum in OIS and PDIS is finite because the reward set, horizon, and dataset are finite. An observed pair with $\mu(A_t^i\mid S_t^i)=0$ lies on a behavior-null trajectory atom by [F1]. Since the trajectory space, horizon, and sample size are finite, the event that any observed pair has zero behavior propensity is a finite union of null events.
